text.p: Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) said on Monday it was not worried by the prospect of competition to its local mobile phone and paging services and expected to gain more customers as those markets grew.
SingTel's monopoly of mobile telephones and pagers in Singapore will end on April 1 when one new competitor enters the mobile phone market and three new firms compete for paging customers.
But Raphael Leong, SingTel executive vice president in charge of both local services, said the markets had plenty of growth potential and there was room enough for more service providers.
"I am not worried," Leong told Reuters in an interview.
"As with any business there will be some people who want to go to try something new. But the market potential is great."

Leong said there were now around 400,000 Singapore mobile phone customers, equivalent to around 13 percent of the island's population of three million, and there were already more than one million pagers in use.

"Every paging user is potentially a mobile phone user for the simple reason that every pager user is a believer in communications and the mobile phone offers additional capability in communications," he said.
"Therefore, there could be another 700-800,000 mobile phone users," he added.
Leong said he thought the penetration rate for pagers, currently around 34 percent, could also rise.
"That could rise to 40-over percent," he said.
Leong declined to estimate how much market share SingTel could lose to its new competitors but analysts say it could be 10-20 percent over a couple of years.
"SingTel are right to believe there is more potential for growth in the handphone market," said John Chessher, regional telecoms analyst at Schroders in Bangkok.
"The handphone market could grow by around 50 percent by 2000. But new competitors could expect to take at least 15 percent of that, once they are established," he said.
Chessher said he thought Singapore's pager market had little room for growth and that competition in this sector could be fierce.
Singapore's second handphone service is MobileOne, a consortium of Britain's Cable & Wireless, Hong Kong Telecommunications, Keppel Telecom and Singapore Press Holdings.
The company has made an aggresive pitch ahead of the launch of its full service next week, offering a range of price reductions and special offers to lure customers away from SingTel.
Leong conceded the new competition would encourage price cuts but said these were an inevitable response to a newly introduced and evolving technology.

He said Singapore's mobile phone charges had fallen substantially over the last three years despite SingTel's monopoly. Charges for a "minimum user" of 100 minutes of air time a month had dropped to only Singapore $46 (US$32) a month from S$70, he said.

"Our prices have come down regardless of whether we have competition or not," he said. "As a sole provider in the past we have always concentrated on trying to attract more mobile phone users, and that will continue."
He declined to discuss SingTel's margins or profits from the mobile phone or paging services.
-- Singapore newsroom (65 8703199)
